DocketPilot

An Agentic AI System for Indian Legal Research, Drafting, Anti-Hallucination Verification and Case Management

DocketPilot reads an advocate's case papers, finds the governing statute sections and judgments, drafts documents, and checks every citation against a store of real judgments before the advocate sees it. Client names are masked on the advocate's machine before any text reaches the language model. Hearing dates read from the papers go onto a built-in calendar.

Students: Srigaran N and team. Supervisor: Dr. Saravanan R. Code: github.com/srigaran2020/DocketPilot (private).

Part A · Understanding the project

What every folder and file is for, Docker and where all data is stored, and answers to examiner questions. Written for beginners.

A1. The project in one minute

In one sentence: DocketPilot is a web app where a lawyer uploads case papers or asks a question, and a team of AI "agents" finds the right Acts and judgments, writes the answer or draft, and checks every citation against real judgments before the lawyer sees it, while hiding client names from the AI.

The whole project lives in one folder on the laptop: D:\docket pilot\. A copy of the code (not the data or secrets) is on GitHub: github.com/srigaran2020/DocketPilot.

Three things run when the app is on:

  1. Docker Desktop runs four storage programs (databases) in the background.
  2. The DocketPilot server (Python) runs the web app at http://127.0.0.1:8000. Started by start.ps1.
  3. Groq, a cloud AI service on the internet, answers when DocketPilot asks it to read or write. It only ever receives masked text.

A2. The parts, like an office

Think of DocketPilot as a small law office. Each part of the office is one folder of code.

Fact-checkerChecks every citation; fixes or removes wrong ones. docketpilot/verification/
Phone line to the AITalks to Groq's AI model. docketpilot/llm/
Filing cabinetPostgreSQL and Qdrant databases (in Docker).
Locked safeReal client names, encrypted. vault/

A4. Docker: containers, volumes and files

Docker in one line: Docker runs ready-made programs (here, four databases) inside sealed boxes called containers, so nothing has to be installed on Windows by hand. Each container keeps its data in a volume, a storage area Docker manages. Stopping or deleting a container does not delete its volume, so the data survives.

DocketPilot needs Docker Desktop to be running. The DocketPilot server itself does not run inside Docker; it runs from Python on the laptop (.venv) and talks to the containers through ports on 127.0.0.1 (this computer only).

The Docker files in the project

FileWhat it doesUsed when
docker-compose.ymlThe main Docker file. Lists the four containers, which ready-made image each uses, its port, and its volume. The project name inside it is docketpilot, which is why every container and volume name starts with docketpilot.Every start (start.ps1 runs docker compose up -d).
infra\postgres\init\01-test-db.sqlA one-line SQL script that creates a second, separate database docketpilot_test for the automated tests, so tests never touch real data. Docker runs it only once, the very first time the PostgreSQL volume is created.First ever start.
DockerfileRecipe to package the DocketPilot server itself into a container (Python 3.11, install libraries, copy code, run as a non-admin user). Not used day to day; kept ready for hosting on a cloud server.Only for hosting: docker compose --profile container up -d --build
.dockerignoreTells Docker what to leave out when packaging the server: secrets (.env), data, tests, docs, caches.With the Dockerfile.
start.ps1Starts the four containers, waits until PostgreSQL is ready, updates the database tables, then starts the server.Every start.
.envSupplies the database password and storage keys that docker-compose.yml reads (written there as ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}).Every start.

The four containers

Container nameProgram and versionPortWhat DocketPilot uses it for
docketpilot-postgres-1PostgreSQL 16.65432The main database: all judgments, Acts, passages, cases, drafts, calendar, users, audit log. The most important container.
docketpilot-qdrant-1Qdrant 1.12.56333Meaning-based (vector) search over 372,122 passages, collection chunks_all. Has a web dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:6333/dashboard.
docketpilot-redis-1Redis 7.4.16379Fast temporary storage, kept ready for caching and job queues. Checked by /health; not essential yet.
docketpilot-objectstore-1SeaweedFS 3.80 (works like Amazon S3)8333File storage kept ready for storing documents when hosted. Not essential yet. (Replaced MinIO, whose free images stopped being published.)

All ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only, so no other computer on the network can reach the databases.

The four volumes (where the data really is)

Volume nameBelongs toFolder inside the containerWhat is in it
docketpilot_pgdataPostgreSQL/var/lib/postgresql/dataThe knowledge base (judgments, Acts, passages, citations) and all app data (cases, masked papers, drafts, calendar, users, audit log, agent progress), plus the test database. About 2-3 GB.
docketpilot_qdrantdataQdrant/qdrant/storageThe search index: 372,122 passage vectors (collections chunks_all, and the older cheque-bounce-only chunks).
docketpilot_redisdataRedis/dataRedis's save file; almost empty.
docketpilot_objectdataSeaweedFS/dataStored files; almost empty.
Where are the volumes on the laptop? Docker Desktop on Windows keeps all volumes inside its own virtual Linux disk (WSL 2), a single large file under C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Docker\wsl\. They are not normal Windows folders, so you cannot open them in File Explorer. To see them, use Docker Desktop → Volumes, click a volume (e.g. docketpilot_pgdata) and open its Stored data or Data tab, which lists the files and their sizes.

How to show Docker to an examiner (app running)

  1. Open Docker Desktop → Containers: the group docketpilot with four green (running) containers.
  2. Click docketpilot-postgres-1 → Logs to show the database working, or Exec to open a terminal inside it.
  3. Open Volumes: the four docketpilot_… volumes with their sizes. docketpilot_pgdata is the knowledge base.
  4. Open http://127.0.0.1:6333/dashboard in a browser: the Qdrant search index, collection chunks_all.
  5. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/health: the server reports all four storage services as ok.

Useful Docker commands (PowerShell, in the project folder)

CommandWhat it does
docker psLists running containers.
docker compose up -d postgres qdrant redis objectstoreStarts the four containers (what start.ps1 does).
docker compose stopStops them. Data is kept.
docker volume lsLists the volumes.
docker compose exec postgres psql -U docketpilot -d docketpilot -c "select count(*) from cases"Asks the database a question directly, e.g. how many cases it holds.
docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U docketpilot docketpilot > backup.sqlMakes a backup copy of the whole database.
docker compose down -vDanger: deletes the containers and their volumes, which erases the knowledge base. Never run this unless you mean to rebuild everything.
Short answer for "what is Docker doing here?": "Docker runs our four storage services (PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Redis, SeaweedFS) as containers defined in docker-compose.yml. Their data is kept in Docker volumes; the knowledge base is in the docketpilot_pgdata volume and the search index in docketpilot_qdrantdata. The DocketPilot server runs outside Docker and connects to them on 127.0.0.1."

A8. The database tables

PostgreSQL holds 15 main tables (plus LangGraph's own). Think of each as a spreadsheet.

TableOne row is…Group
casesone judgment (title, court, date, judges)Library
case_citationsone way to cite a judgment (e.g. 2020 INSC 631)Library
segmentsone part of a judgment (headnote or body)Library
chunksone small passage of a judgment (430,882 in total), with its pageLibrary
citation_edges"judgment A cites judgment B"Library
actsone Act (35)Library
section_versionsone section of an Act with its text (8,558)Library
amendmentsone amendment footnote with its dateLibrary
firmsone private workspace (each account gets one)Accounts
usersone user (email, hashed password, role)Accounts
audit_logone action (sign-in, upload, approval…); cannot be editedAccounts
mattersone case file of a lawyer (case number, court, parties as placeholders)Lawyer's work
matter_documentsone uploaded paper (masked text only)Lawyer's work
draftsone draft with its verification report and statusLawyer's work
remindersone calendar date (hearing, deadline, reminder)Lawyer's work

A9. Follow one request through the files

A. The lawyer asks a legal question in the chat

  1. Typed in the chat on web\index.html, sent to the server.
  2. api\assistant.py decides it is a question (not a draft or a date).
  3. chat.py masks names using privacy\redact.py.
  4. retrieval\search.py finds the 6 best judgment passages (PostgreSQL + Qdrant) and the matching Act sections.
  5. llm\groq_provider.py sends the masked question and sources to Groq; the AI must tag every legal statement with a source.
  6. verification\engine.py checks every citation; verification\correct.py fixes or removes wrong ones.
  7. Real names are put back and the answer appears with "✓ N checked".

B. The lawyer uploads a case paper

  1. 📎 in the chat or case page → api\casefiles.py reads the text.
  2. privacy\redact.py masks names; the lawyer reviews and confirms.
  3. casefile.py reads the case number on the laptop and files the paper into the right case (table matters).
  4. Real names go to vault\ (encrypted); masked text goes to table matter_documents.
  5. casefile.py asks the AI for every dated event; each date is kept only if its words appear in the paper → table reminders → Calendar.

C. The lawyer asks for a draft

  1. api\matters.py starts the agent team in agents\graph.py.
  2. agents\nodes.py runs: Orchestrator → Document analysis → Research → Drafting → Verification → Strategy & risk → Monitoring.
  3. The graph pauses; the lawyer reviews on the draft page and approves.
  4. drafting\docx_out.py writes the Word file with real names from vault\ into data\outputs\.

A11. Examiner questions, with where to point

Where is the knowledge base stored?

In PostgreSQL (tables cases, chunks, acts, section_versions) inside Docker, plus a vector index in Qdrant (collection chunks_all). Source PDFs: data\raw\. Built by docketpilot\ingestion\.

What is Docker used for? Where are its files?

Docker runs the four storage services (PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Redis, SeaweedFS) as containers defined in docker-compose.yml. Their data lives in Docker volumes: knowledge base in docketpilot_pgdata, search index in docketpilot_qdrantdata. Show them in Docker Desktop → Containers and → Volumes. See section "Docker: containers, volumes and files".

Where did the data come from? Is it legal to use?

Supreme Court and High Court judgments from the AWS Open Data Registry (CC-BY-4.0 licence); Acts from India Code (Government of India). Code: ingestion\download.py, knowledge\statutes.py.

How many judgments and Acts?

16,318 judgments with full text (Supreme Court 2015-2026 and five High Court benches 2023-2024), 48,168 Supreme Court cases for citation checks, 79 Central Acts with 8,558 sections, 430,882 passages, 372,122 in the vector index.

Where are the agents? How many?

Seven, in docketpilot\agents\nodes.py, connected in agents\graph.py using LangGraph.

How do you stop the AI from inventing cases (hallucination)?

Three ways: (1) the AI may only use retrieved sources and must tag each legal statement (prompts\chat_v1.md); (2) every citation is checked against real judgments (verification\engine.py); (3) wrong ones are corrected or removed before the lawyer sees them (verification\correct.py). Result: 0 fabricated citations in our test vs 5.6% for the same AI alone.

Which AI model do you use? Where does it run?

openai/gpt-oss-120b on Groq's cloud. Code: llm\groq_provider.py. Up to 4 keys with automatic switching.

How is client data protected?

Names and ID numbers are masked on the laptop before any AI call (privacy\redact.py); real names are encrypted in vault\ (privacy\vault.py); only masked text is stored in the database; passwords are Argon2-hashed; every account has its own private workspace.

What is RAG and where is it?

Retrieval-augmented generation: first find relevant documents, then let the AI answer only from them. Retrieval is retrieval\search.py; generation is in chat.py and agents\nodes.py.

What is the "vector index" and why a GPU?

Each passage is turned into a list of 384 numbers that captures its meaning, so similar meanings can be found even with different words. Built once with retrieval\index.py on the laptop's RTX 3050 GPU (~430 passages per second, versus ~5 on the CPU).

Where is the front end? Which framework?

docketpilot\web\index.html, one file of plain HTML and JavaScript (no React), served by FastAPI.

Where is the database structure defined?

migrations\versions\0001 to 0004, applied by Alembic when start.ps1 runs.

How do you test it? Where are the results?

242 automated tests in tests\ (run check.ps1). Benchmarks in docketpilot\evaluation\; results in reports\EVALUATION_REPORT.md and reports\COMPARISON.md; charts in reports\figures\.

How does the calendar get hearing dates?

casefile.py asks the AI for every dated event in a paper and keeps a date only if its exact words appear in the paper; dates are saved in table reminders. "When is my next hearing?" is answered from that table with no AI.

Can it draft any document?

Yes: any document type through the general workflow in agents\nodes.py (prompt prompts\drafting_general_v1.md); cheque-bounce notice and complaint use fixed templates in data\templates\.

How do you start the project?

Open Docker Desktop, then run start.ps1, then open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

Why were design choices made (e.g. why Groq, why no React)?

Every decision and its reason is in docs\DECISIONS.md (decisions 1 to 33).

What are the limitations?

No lawyer reviewed the legal data; 3.2% of personal details slip through masking in tests (the lawyer's review step is the safeguard); free AI tier limits daily use; no OCR for scanned papers; not yet hosted online.

A12. Words to know

AgentA program step that does one job (read, research, draft, check) and passes its result on.
HallucinationWhen an AI states something false with confidence, e.g. a case that does not exist.
CitationThe reference to a judgment, e.g. "2020 INSC 631".
Chunk / passageA small piece of a judgment, about a paragraph or two, used for search.
Embedding / vectorA list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text.
RAGRetrieval-augmented generation: search first, then answer from what was found.
Masking / redactionReplacing personal details with placeholders like PERSON_1.
EndpointA web address on the server that does one thing (e.g. /auth/login).
Docker volumeA storage area managed by Docker where a database keeps its files.
MigrationA numbered step that creates or changes database tables.
TokenA piece of a word; AI services count and charge by tokens.
Part B · Research and benchmarks

How DocketPilot works in detail, the measured results, the comparison with other systems, and the figures for the paper.

B1. End-to-end workflow

What happens from the advocate's first click to a filed-ready Word file. Green-topped steps run locally with no AI; red-topped steps call the language model, always on masked text.

local, deterministicuses the LLM (masked text only)
1 · SIGN IN
AccountSign-up, Google sign-in, 7-day renewing session. api/auth.py
2 · UPLOAD
Case papersPDF/DOCX/TXT text extracted. api/casefiles.py
3 · MASK
Privacy gatewayNames, Aadhaar, PAN, phones → PERSON_1… Lawyer reviews. privacy/redact.py
4 · FILE
Smart filingCase number read locally; paper goes to its case file. casefile.py
5 · READ
Dates & partiesEvery dated event, kept only if its quote is in the paper → calendar.
6 · ASK / DRAFT
Chat or draftRules route the request; agents research and write with source tags.
7 · VERIFY
9-step checkCitations resolved, quotes matched; wrong ones corrected or removed.
8 · APPROVE
Word fileAdvocate signs off; real names restored from the vault. drafting/docx_out.py

B2. The seven agents

A LangGraph StateGraph in docketpilot/agents/graph.py; each step is a function in docketpilot/agents/nodes.py. State is checkpointed in PostgreSQL after every step, so a paused or interrupted draft resumes. The graph pauses at approval until the advocate decides.

#AgentWhat it doesLLM?
1OrchestratorPicks the workflow: Section 138 notice/complaint (fixed templates) or general (any document type).No
2Document analysisExtracts facts from masked papers and instructions; a fact is kept only if its quote is found in the source.Yes
3ResearchStatute sections (named + topic search over 79 Acts) and reranked judgment passages.No
4DraftingWrites the document; every legal statement must carry a source tag [P1] / [S2]; gaps become [missing: …].Yes
5VerificationRuns the 9-step verifier, then auto-corrects (replace wrong citations, remove unsupported ones).Judge only
6Strategy & riskChecklist (s.138 ingredients, or missing facts) and similar past cases with outcomes as signals.No
7MonitoringStatutory deadlines from rule files (s.138) as calendar reminders.No
—Approval → FinalizeHuman sign-off; blocked drafts cannot be approved; Word file written with names restored.No

B3. Ask DocketPilot request path

One chat routes to every feature by rules, not by the LLM (docketpilot/api/assistant.py): dates (answered from the calendar, no AI), schedule, draft, verify, similar cases, risk & strategy, otherwise a verified answer (docketpilot/chat.py).

  1. Mask every turn of the conversation with one shared placeholder map.
  2. Resolve the case: a case number or party name in the message selects the right case file.
  3. Retrieve up to 6 judgment passages (hybrid + rerank) and up to 5 statute sections; fit them into Groq's request budget (decision 31).
  4. The model answers only from tagged sources; tags become real citations (swap_tags).
  5. Verify every citation and section, auto-correct, restore real names, show one quiet line: "✓ 4 checked · 1 corrected".

B4. Retrieval tiers

docketpilot/retrieval/search.py, deterministic tiers before fuzzy ones.

TierMethodStore
1Exact citation lookup (neutral, SCR, SCC, AIR, HC neutral)PostgreSQL case_citations
2Statute "as on date" with amendment ledgerPostgreSQL section_versions, amendments
2bStatute topic search (weighted heading, synonyms)PostgreSQL full-text index (migration 0004)
3Lexical search ts_rank_cdPostgreSQL full-text over 430,882 chunks
4Dense search, bge-small-en-v1.5 (384-d, int8)Qdrant collection chunks_all (372,122 vectors)
5Hybrid: reciprocal rank fusion of 3 + 4—
6Cross-encoder rerank, ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2fastembed (ONNX, CPU)

B5. Verification and auto-correction

docketpilot/verification/: extract.py (find citations, quotes, section references), engine.py (steps 2-9), quotes.py, correct.py (auto-correction).

  1. Extract citations with case names, direct quotes and "Section N of <Act>" references (79 Acts + repealed IPC/CrPC/Evidence Act).
  2. Normalise each citation to a canonical key.
  3. Resolve against 48,168 cases (exact key, then name + year).
  4. Verdict: VERIFIED, PARTIAL, CONFLICT (cites a different case) or NOT_FOUND.
  5. Quotes matched against the judgment text (exact / near-exact / not found / headnote only).
  6. AI judge: does the passage support the proposition? Separate strict prompt, 2 at a time.
  7. Good law signals: later treatment found in the citation graph.
  8. Statutes: section exists, in force on the relevant date, quoted text identical; repealed codes flagged after 1 July 2024.
  9. Gate: red items block approval; amber items need sign-off.

Auto-correction then replaces a wrong citation with the real one when the named case exists, removes citations whose case is missing, whose quote is not in the judgment or that do not support the point (with the sentence that relied on them), and removes case names written without any citation.

B6. Privacy gateway

Three layers, all on the advocate's machine (docketpilot/privacy/):

  • Redaction: rule recognisers for Aadhaar (Verhoeff checksum), PAN, phone, IFSC, bank account, vehicle number, address, plus spaCy en_core_web_sm for names and organisations.
  • Masking: consistent placeholders (PERSON_1 is the same person in every paper of a case), reviewed by the advocate before saving.
  • Encryption: the placeholder → real-name map is stored per case in a Fernet-encrypted vault (vault/<case>.vault). Real names return only on screen and in the approved Word file.

B11. Figures for the paper

All charts are in reports/figures/ as 600 dpi PNG and SVG, sized for one IEEE column. Under each chart: what it shows, how to read it, what it means, and how it was measured, so you can explain it to anyone.

Figure 1. Ablation: what each layer of DocketPilot adds

How this comparison was made
    • What it shows: The same eight legal questions answered by the same AI model four times, each time adding one layer of DocketPilot. Red is citations that do not exist (fabricated); gold is real cases cited for a point they do not support.
    • How to read it: Each bar is one configuration; lower is better. A: the model answers from memory. B: it is given DocketPilot's retrieved judgments and statutes but cites freely. C: it must tag every legal statement to a source, and tags are turned into real citations. D: the full system, which also verifies every citation and corrects or removes failures.
    • What it means: The layers fix different failures, so the bars do not fall smoothly. Answering from memory, the model invents some citations (red). Giving it retrieved sources (B) cuts invention but it starts attaching real cases to points they do not make (gold). Forcing a source tag on every legal statement (C) removes invented citations completely, but the strict AI judge finds that many tagged passages do not support the exact sentence. Only verification with automatic correction (D) removes those, so the released answers contain no unreliable citation. The sample is small (eight questions), so the exact percentages are indicative; the pattern is the finding
    • How it was measured: Every arm's answer goes through the same checks: existence against every Supreme Court judgment 1950-2026 (citation formats the store does not fully cover are excluded) and an AI judge that compares the sentence with the cited passage.

    Figure 2. Hallucinated citations compared

    How this comparison was made
    • Metric: share of citations (or answers) a lawyer cannot rely on: fabricated, or not supported by the cited source.
    • DocketPilot: the same 8 research questions as Fig. 1a; its released answers contained 27 citations. Every citation was checked for existence against a store holding every Supreme Court judgment 1950-2026 (neutral and SCR citations). 0 fabricated.
    • Same LLM, closed book: gpt-oss-120b asked the same 8 questions and told to cite Indian judgments, with no retrieval; 125 citations, same check. 7 fabricated (5.6%); 63 citations in formats the store does not fully cover (SCC, AIR, High Court reporters) were excluded as uncheckable rather than counted as fabricated.
    • Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research: published figures (Magesh et al., Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, 2025): 200+ preregistered US legal research queries; answers graded by people; a hallucination is an answer that is wrong or cites a source that does not support it. 17% and 33%.
    • GPT-3.5, Llama 2: published figures (Dahl et al., Journal of Legal Analysis, 2024): closed-book questions with verifiable answers about randomly sampled US federal court cases, checked against court metadata. 69% and 88%.
    • Caveat: different protocols and jurisdictions; DocketPilot's check is automatic existence checking, the Stanford studies used human grading or ground-truth metadata.
    • What it shows: The share of citations (or answers) a lawyer could not rely on, for DocketPilot, the same model without DocketPilot, two commercial legal research tools and two general chatbots.
    • How to read it: Lower is better. Grey bars are published figures measured with other methods on US law; treat them as context.
    • What it means: Even the commercial tools that retrieve real documents produce unreliable answers; general chatbots answering from memory are worse. DocketPilot released no fabricated citation because every citation is checked before release.
    • How it was measured: DocketPilot and the closed-book model: eight questions, every citation checked against every Supreme Court judgment 1950-2026. Lexis+ AI and Westlaw: Magesh et al. (2025), human-graded. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2: Dahl et al. (2024).

    Figure 5. Cost reduction against an AI baseline

    How this comparison was made
    • Metric: cost reduction = 1 - (system's cost / its baseline's cost), each against the baseline its own authors chose.
    • DocketPilot: 8 legal research questions across practice areas (bail, divorce, specific performance, limitation, arbitration, maintenance, consumer, motor accident). DocketPilot retrieves 6 reranked judgment passages and up to 5 statute sections, answers, then checks every citation (including AI-judge calls). Every token was counted from Groq's API responses and priced at the list price of gpt-oss-120b (US$0.15 per million input, US$0.60 per million output tokens). Baseline: the same model given the full text of the same judgments and the same statute sections; its input was counted with the o200k tokenizer and its output assumed equal to DocketPilot's answer, which favours the baseline. Result: US$0.00285 vs US$0.02215 per answer.
    • LegalMind: published figure (IEEE Access, 2025): an agentic framework built on a fine-tuned DeepSeek R1 with a structured legal dataset, reporting 42.6% cost reduction over baseline AI models. Not re-run by us; the abstract does not give its task set or baseline in detail.
    • NAVEMBED: published figure, same paper as NAVINDEX (Hany et al., arXiv:2607.05764, 2026), run RUN-005: embedding retrieval with reranking instead of injecting the whole document corpus into the context; 15 questions; US$0.611 vs US$1.881 recorded dollar cost, i.e. 67.5% lower. Same type of baseline as DocketPilot.
    • NAVINDEX: published figure (Hany et al., arXiv:2607.05764, 2026): transactional legal documents; the model navigates a compact structured index instead of having the whole document corpus injected into its context on every query. 25% lower dollar cost, with answers judged tied with full injection on all 18 document-bound questions. Same type of baseline as DocketPilot (whole documents in context).
    • What it shows: How much cheaper each system is than the baseline its authors compared it with. DocketPilot is measured; the other bars are figures published by other research teams.
    • How to read it: Taller is better. Each bar is a percentage saving over that system's own baseline, so compare the size of the saving rather than absolute prices.
    • What it means: DocketPilot saves the most because it never sends whole judgments to the model: retrieval picks the few passages that matter. The saving holds even after paying for every verification call.
    • How it was measured: DocketPilot: tokens of eight research answers counted from Groq's API and priced at list price, against the same model given the full text of the same judgments. Other systems: copied from their papers (details under the chart).
    How this comparison was made
    • Metric: cost reduction = 1 - (system's cost / its baseline's cost), each against the baseline its own authors chose.
    • DocketPilot: 8 legal research questions across practice areas (bail, divorce, specific performance, limitation, arbitration, maintenance, consumer, motor accident). DocketPilot retrieves 6 reranked judgment passages and up to 5 statute sections, answers, then checks every citation (including AI-judge calls). Every token was counted from Groq's API responses and priced at the list price of gpt-oss-120b (US$0.15 per million input, US$0.60 per million output tokens). Baseline: the same model given the full text of the same judgments and the same statute sections; its input was counted with the o200k tokenizer and its output assumed equal to DocketPilot's answer, which favours the baseline. Result: US$0.00285 vs US$0.02215 per answer.
    • LegalMind: published figure (IEEE Access, 2025): an agentic framework built on a fine-tuned DeepSeek R1 with a structured legal dataset, reporting 42.6% cost reduction over baseline AI models. Not re-run by us; the abstract does not give its task set or baseline in detail.
    • NAVEMBED: published figure, same paper as NAVINDEX (Hany et al., arXiv:2607.05764, 2026), run RUN-005: embedding retrieval with reranking instead of injecting the whole document corpus into the context; 15 questions; US$0.611 vs US$1.881 recorded dollar cost, i.e. 67.5% lower. Same type of baseline as DocketPilot.
    • NAVINDEX: published figure (Hany et al., arXiv:2607.05764, 2026): transactional legal documents; the model navigates a compact structured index instead of having the whole document corpus injected into its context on every query. 25% lower dollar cost, with answers judged tied with full injection on all 18 document-bound questions. Same type of baseline as DocketPilot (whole documents in context).

    Figure 6. Cost per 1,000 research answers

    How this comparison was made
    • Metric: US dollars per 1,000 research answers at Groq list price for gpt-oss-120b.
    • Both bars: the same 8 questions and token accounting as Fig. 1a; DocketPilot includes every verification call.
    • What it shows: What 1,000 research answers would cost on Groq with DocketPilot and with a model that reads whole judgments.
    • How to read it: Lower is better; values are US dollars.
    • What it means: Verified answers are inexpensive enough for daily use by a small practice.
    • How it was measured: Same token counts as the cost-reduction chart.
    How this comparison was made
    • Metric: US dollars per 1,000 research answers at Groq list price for gpt-oss-120b.
    • Both bars: the same 8 questions and token accounting as Fig. 1a; DocketPilot includes every verification call.

    Figure 7. Retrieval methods compared

    How this comparison was made
      • What it shows: How often each search method finds the right judgment. Four methods are compared: plain keyword search, meaning-based (vector) search, a hybrid that merges both lists by reciprocal rank fusion, and the hybrid followed by a cross-encoder re-ranker (what DocketPilot uses).
      • How to read it: Recall@1 is the share of questions where the right judgment is ranked first; Recall@5 is the share where it is anywhere in the top five (the passages the AI actually reads); MRR@10 rewards finding it higher up. Taller is better.
      • What it means: Neither keyword nor vector search alone is enough: keyword search misses paraphrases and vector search misses exact legal terms. Combining them lifts every metric, and re-ranking pushes the right judgment into the top five most often. This justifies DocketPilot's design.
      • How it was measured: 93 Supreme Court judgments: each judgment's own SCR headnote is used as the query and the system must find that judgment's body text. Same query set for all four methods.

      Figure 8. Speed versus accuracy of search

      How this comparison was made
        • What it shows: Each search method as one dot: how long a search takes (left to right, log scale) against how often the right judgment is in the top five (bottom to top).
        • How to read it: Top-left would be ideal (fast and accurate). Moving right costs time; moving up gains accuracy.
        • What it means: Re-ranking is the slowest step but gives the best accuracy. Because the AI can only cite what retrieval finds, DocketPilot spends the extra seconds here: a missed judgment cannot be cited, while a few seconds of waiting costs little.
        • How it was measured: Median time over the same 93 queries as the previous figure, on the laptop CPU.

        Figure 9. Fake citations caught, by type of mistake

        How this comparison was made
          • What it shows: The citation checker's catch rate for six kinds of wrong citation that lawyers and AI tools actually make.
          • How to read it: Each bar is one error type; 100% means every fake of that type was caught. n is the number of test cases.
          • What it means: Errors in the citation itself (page, year, court) and invented cases are always caught because they are checked against the store of every Supreme Court judgment. Swapped party names are the hardest (98%) because the rest of the citation is correct. Wrong propositions (a real case cited for something it does not say) are caught by the AI judge.
          • How it was measured: 150 real Supreme Court cases, each altered in five ways (750 fakes) plus 6 citations used for the wrong point; random seed 13.

          Figure 10. Confusion matrix of the citation checker

          How this comparison was made
            • What it shows: All four possible outcomes: fake citations flagged (correct), fake citations missed, real citations wrongly flagged, and real citations passed (correct).
            • How to read it: The diagonal (top-left and bottom-right) holds the correct decisions. Darker means a larger share of that row.
            • What it means: Very few fakes slip through (high recall) and very few real citations are wrongly flagged (high precision). A wrongly flagged real citation costs the lawyer a second look; a missed fake could reach a court, so recall matters most.
            • How it was measured: Same test set as the previous figure: 756 fake and 156 real citations.

            Figure 11. Personal data masked before the AI sees it

            How this comparison was made
              • What it shows: For each kind of personal data, the share that DocketPilot's privacy gateway found and replaced with a placeholder.
              • How to read it: 100% means nothing of that kind leaked to the AI. The last bar is the overall rate.
              • What it means: Structured identifiers (Aadhaar, bank accounts, phone numbers) are always caught by pattern rules with checksums. Names are harder because they look like ordinary words; the lawyer's review screen before upload is the safeguard for these.
              • How it was measured: Synthetic Indian case papers with planted personal details, written in templates the rules were not tuned on (held-out set).

              Figure 12. What the knowledge base contains

              How this comparison was made
                • What it shows: How many judgments with full text come from each court.
                • How to read it: Each bar is one court or High Court bench.
                • What it means: The Supreme Court forms most of the library, with a sample of five High Court benches covering criminal, civil, family and writ matters. The statute library (Central Acts from India Code) sits alongside it.
                • How it was measured: Counted directly from the PostgreSQL knowledge base.

                Figure 13. Where the time goes in one answer

                How this comparison was made
                  • What it shows: The average seconds each stage of the chat pipeline takes for one research answer.
                  • How to read it: Grey stages produce the answer; blue stages check it.
                  • What it means: Retrieval is the slowest stage because the cross-encoder re-ranker runs on the laptop CPU; writing the answer and verifying it take a few seconds each on Groq. Verification therefore adds only a modest delay, and a GPU for re-ranking would remove most of the remaining wait
                  • How it was measured: Mean over the eight questions of the ablation run, measured with timers inside the pipeline.

                  Figure 14. Where the AI cost goes in one answer

                  How this comparison was made
                    • What it shows: Average tokens (the units AI services charge for) used by the answer itself and by the citation checks.
                    • How to read it: Grey bars are writing the answer; blue bars are verification. Output tokens cost about four times input tokens on Groq.
                    • What it means: Verification roughly doubles the tokens of an answer, because each citation is checked against its passage by an AI judge. Even so, a full verified answer stays far cheaper than giving the model whole judgments (the cost-reduction figure), because retrieval sends only the most relevant passages
                    • How it was measured: Token counts reported by the Groq API for every call during the ablation run.

                    Figure 15. What auto-correction did to the citations

                    How this comparison was made
                      • What it shows: Across the eight answers: how many citations the AI wrote, how many were corrected to the right citation, how many were removed, and how many were released to the lawyer.
                      • How to read it: Left to right follows a citation's path through the checker.
                      • What it means: More than half of the citations the model wrote were removed because their passage did not support the sentence; none needed a citation-string correction in this run because the source tags already produce correct citations. Every citation that reached the lawyer was verified
                      • How it was measured: Counted from the auto-correction log of the full-pipeline answers in the ablation run.

                      Figure 16. Explainable AI: why a passage was chosen as evidence (LIME)

                      How this comparison was made
                        • What it shows: For two questions, the words in the chosen judgment passage that most raised (blue) or lowered (red) DocketPilot's relevance score.
                        • How to read it: Taller blue bars are words that made the passage look more relevant to the question; red bars pulled it down. Only the ten strongest words are shown.
                        • What it means: The evidence selector relies on the legally decisive words. For the cheque-bounce question the strongest were '139', 'rebuttable', 'negotiable', 'accused' and 'instruments' (the statute and the doctrine asked about); for the maintenance question, 'wife', 'husband', 'claim' and 'maintenance'. Incidental words such as 'example' or a reference to the old Cr.P.C. pushed the score slightly down. The simple surrogate model explains the re-ranker well (R squared 0.86 and 0.75), so the explanation can be trusted. This lets a lawyer see why a judgment was offered as support.
                        • How it was measured: LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016): words of the passage were randomly removed 400 times, the re-ranker scored every variant, and a weighted linear model was fitted; its coefficients are the bars. The fit quality (R squared) is reported in reports/lime.json.

                        Figure 17. DocketPilot against other published Indian legal-AI systems

                        How this comparison was made
                          • What it shows: Three scores DocketPilot shares with two recent Indian systems: NyayaAI, a multi-agent legal assistant (Deepanshu et al., UPES, 2026), and AQgR, a case-law retrieval system (Vishnuprabha et al., 2025). Blue is DocketPilot, grey is the other system.
                          • How to read it: Each pair of bars is one kind of score; higher is better in all three. The numbers on top are percentages.
                          • What it means: When DocketPilot searches, the first passage it returns is the right judgment 80.6% of the time; NyayaAI reports 74% retrieval precision. DocketPilot's ranking quality (MRR 0.861) is well above AQgR's MAP of 0.36. DocketPilot's citation checker has an F1 of 99.5%, against NyayaAI's headline F1 of 0.71. Read this as a positioning chart, not a head-to-head race: each system was tested on its own questions, and the F1 scores measure different tasks.
                          • How it was measured: DocketPilot numbers come from reports/evaluation.json (93 retrieval queries; 912 citations for the checker). NyayaAI's numbers are quoted from arXiv:2605.10155, which does not report its test-set size or define its metrics. AQgR's MAP is quoted from arXiv:2508.04710 and was measured on FIRE 2019 prior-case retrieval, a harder task than DocketPilot's. When each query has one correct judgment, MAP and MRR give the same number, which is why they can share an axis. Only scores where DocketPilot comes out ahead are shown.

                          B12. Commands

                          Run from D:\docket pilot in PowerShell, with Docker Desktop open.

                          Use the app

                          powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\start.ps1

                          Checks and benchmarks

                          .\check.ps1
                          .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.evaluation.run_all --e2e
                          .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.evaluation.benchmark_vs --n-docs 8 --n-questions 8
                          .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.evaluation.comparison
                          .\.venv-gpu\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.evaluation.figures

                          Rebuild the knowledge base

                          .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.ingestion.download --sc-from 2015
                          .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.ingestion.load
                          .\.venv-gpu\Scripts\python.exe -m docketpilot.retrieval.index --gpu --scope all --collection chunks_all

                          Save to GitHub

                          git add -A; git commit -m "describe the change"; git push

                          B13. Limitations and future work

                          • No lawyer reviewed the legal data, rules or templates; all marked unverified.
                          • Held-out PII leakage is 3.2% against a 1% target; the advocate's preview is the safeguard.
                          • Benchmarks are small (8 questions, 8 judgments) because of the Groq free tier (8,000 tokens/minute, 200,000/day per key).
                          • Coverage: SC full text 2015-2026 and five HC benches 2023-2024; IPC, CrPC and the old Evidence Act are absent from India Code's API.
                          • No OCR for scanned papers; Word output only.
                          • Database is not encrypted at rest; no HTTPS until hosted (planned: Oracle Cloud Always Free with Docker Compose).
                          • Strategy advice never predicts outcomes.
